activity.notes: Seventeenth-century missionary material and modern Amazonian scholarship identify Maria Moaçara as a high-status Tapajó woman described in colonial terminology as a hereditary 'princess' and principal oracle who mediated between Indigenous people and Portuguese missionaries. A modern scholarly edition places a notable intervention around 1677. ATLAS therefore registers Maria Moaçara with the Tapajó and a c.1677 representative point; it does not reproduce the game-mod attribution that makes 'Cunhã Moaçara' a ruler of Marajoara, and it does not treat the Nheengatu expression cunhã moaçara ('woman of great nobility') as proof of a sovereign royal office.

sources.title: Revisitando os alter egos: figuras sobrepostas na iconografia Konduri e sua relação com o xamanismo — Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi
sources.citation_text: The peer-reviewed article identifies Maria Moaçara in the Jesuit Tapajó settlement as a female shaman/oracle who mediated relations between Indigenous people and the Portuguese.

sources.title: A ‘Relação’ de Jacinto de Carvalho (1719), um texto inédito de etnografia amazônica — scholarly edition
sources.citation_text: The scholarly edition distinguishes the title/expression Cunhã Moacara ('woman of great nobility') and notes Maria Moacara, described as a hereditary 'princess' of the Tapajó and principal oracle, intervening around 1677.

review_context.correction_note: Correct the mod's Marajoaran ruler attribution to the historically documented Maria Moaçara of the Tapajó.
